About this citation

Two parts that are read as one work: the camp memoir and the exposition of logotherapy, written later and appended. The original German title is 'Nevertheless, Say Yes to Life', and the English title was the publisher's.

### Exact wording

English (as recorded here)

“Everything can be taken from a man but one thing: the last of the human freedoms — to choose one's attitude in any given set of circumstances, to choose one's own way.”

German

“Dem Menschen kann alles genommen werden, nur nicht eines: die letzte der menschlichen Freiheiten — unter welchen Umständen auch immer die eigene Einstellung zu wählen, seinen eigenen Weg.”

Frankl wrote in German; the widely quoted English is the standard translation of Man's Search for Meaning. Wording varies slightly by edition of the English text.

#### Forms in circulation that differ

-   “Everything can be taken from a man but one thing: the last of the human freedoms — to choose one's attitude in any given set of circumstances.”
-   “The last of the human freedoms is to choose one's attitude in any given set of circumstances.”

### Attribution notes

Viktor Frankl, Man's Search for Meaning (originally …trotzdem Ja zum Leben sagen). The line belongs to his account of camp experience and logotherapy's claim about attitude; clipping it to “choose your attitude” without the “last freedom” framing turns a claim forged under extremity into generic positivity.

#### About Viktor Frankl

Viktor Frankl (1905–1997) founded logotherapy, arguing that the search for meaning is a primary human motivation, shaped by his experiences in Nazi concentration camps.

### Interpretation

Frankl writes this as a psychiatrist who had survived the camps, so the claim is clinical rather than inspirational. Everything external — family, property, health, even the ability to work — was in fact taken from the prisoners he describes. What he reports remaining is not optimism but the position one takes toward conditions one did not choose. He calls it the last of the freedoms in a precise sense: it is the one that cannot be removed by any further loss, because its exercise requires nothing external.

#### Why it matters

The claim is narrower than it is usually quoted as being: attitude is not a substitute for action, and Frankl does not suggest that suffering is worthwhile. It marks the point where choice still exists after everything else has been removed.

### Questions readers arrive with

#### What is the source of the quotation “Everything can be taken from a man but…”?

“Everything can be taken from a man but…” comes from Man's Search for Meaning (1946 (as …trotzdem Ja zum Leben sagen); English 1959), attributed to Viktor Frankl.

#### What does Viktor Frankl mean by freedom?

Philosophers distinguish several ideas under the single word freedom. Negative freedom emphasizes non-interference; positive freedom emphasizes the capacity to act according to reasons, virtue, or authentic desire. This passage enters that discussion through freedom, meaning.

#### Is the wording of this Viktor Frankl quotation commonly changed?

The wording recorded here is “Everything can be taken from a man but one thing: the last of the human freedoms — to choose one's attitude in any given set of circumstances, to choose one's own way.” Forms in circulation that differ: Everything can be taken from a man but one thing: the last of the human freedoms — to choose one's attitude in any given set of circumstances. / The last of the human freedoms is to choose one's attitude in any given set of circumstances. The German reads “Dem Menschen kann alles genommen werden, nur nicht eines: die letzte der menschlichen Freiheiten — unter welchen Umständen auch immer die eigene Einstellung zu wählen, seinen eigenen Weg.”

#### Is this quotation attributed correctly?

Viktor Frankl, Man's Search for Meaning (originally …trotzdem Ja zum Leben sagen). The line belongs to his account of camp experience and logotherapy's claim about attitude; clipping it to “choose your attitude” without the “last freedom” framing turns a claim forged under extremity into generic positivity.
